articles.title: The Brazilian victory: left unity and digital autonomy
articles.author: Rezgar Akrawi
articles.content: The leftist leader Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva secured a historic victory in Brazil’s presidential election on October 25, 2026. The result came amid intense political and social polarization and the growing influence of the far right in Brazil and across Latin America, backed by the US far right led by Donald Trump. The significance of this electoral victory extends beyond Lula securing a fourth term. It also lies in the political and organizational experience that helped make it possible, above all the ability of diverse left-wing and progressive forces, with different programs and ideological outlooks, to forge a broad electoral alliance around common ground in confronting the far right. A broad left-wing and progressive alliance despite differences Lula contested the election with the support of the “Brazil Ready for More” alliance, comprising seven left-wing and progressive parties organized into two party federations and two separate parties. The “Brazil of Hope” federation brought together Lula’s Workers’ Party, the Communist Party of Brazil, and the Green Party. The second federation united the Socialism and Liberty Party, which includes socialist and radical-left currents, with the Sustainability Network. The Brazilian Socialist Party and the Democratic Labor Party also joined the alliance, alongside supportive social movements and trade unions. Lula ran with Geraldo Alckmin of the Brazilian Socialist Party as his vice-presidential candidate. The importance of this alliance lies in its ability to bring together communists, socialists, the radical left, social democrats, and Greens despite their disagreements over capitalism, the role of the state, and the limits of social reform. These forces agreed on common electoral objectives while preserving their identities and organizational autonomy. This is one of the most important lessons of the Brazilian experience. Left unity does not require ideological or organizational uniformity. It means being able to work together on common ground while respecting pluralism and differences. Disagreements over Lula’s economic and social policies will naturally persist, including among the forces that supported him at the ballot box. Unity does not mean abandoning criticism or autonomy The Brazilian experience raises an important question for left-wing forces around the world. Why do ideological and organizational differences become barriers to cooperation, despite so much common ground, even when these forces face shared political and class challenges? Pluralism among communists, social democrats, the radical left, environmentalist and feminist currents, and independent leftists can be a source of strength and intellectual and political richness, provided it is managed democratically and constructively, without monopolization, exclusion, or claims to possess the absolute truth. Unity does not require abandoning criticism or offering unconditional acceptance of the policies of governments led by left-wing and progressive alliances. Confronting Capitalism and the far right requires a broad social front The victory demonstrated the importance of connecting the defense of democracy, rights, and freedoms with the economic and social demands of working classes and poor and marginalized communities. Lula drew broad support from lower-income groups and proposed expanding social assistance, improving living conditions, and defending democratic institutions. Confronting capitalism and the far right therefore cannot be confined to elections and party alliances. It requires sustained mass organizations in workplaces, neighborhoods, universities, trade unions, and social movements, together with policies that tackle class inequality and improve the lives of the majority. Digital autonomy: the fifth pillar of the left’s independence The Brazilian election revealed the growing importance of the digital sphere in political struggle. Social media platforms, algorithms, and artificial intelligence have become powerful tools in the hands of capitalist interests for shaping public consciousness and steering political debate. During the campaign, Lula’s supporters submitted complaints and evidence supporting allegations that Meta, the company that owns Facebook, Instagram, and other platforms, showed digital bias in favor of his opponent. The company acknowledged “technical problems.” The dispute reached Brazil’s electoral court, which issued a ruling requiring Meta to apply equal standards to the candidates. The problem is not confined to Brazil. During Colombia’s most recent presidential election in 2026, journalistic investigations uncovered coordinated accounts and AI-generated fake videos targeting the left-wing camp , as well as shortcomings and bias in the platforms’ oversight of political advertising and content. In Germany, Elon Musk, the owner of X, publicly endorsed the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) during the 2025 election. He used his platform to promote the party’s positions and host its leaders, while several studies found a clear bias in the reach of the party’s content on the platform . Proving deliberate algorithmic bias is difficult because proprietary algorithms give capitalist corporations exclusive control over information about how they work and how content is ranked, amplified, or restricted. Without transparency, independent public and legal oversight, and access to the data needed for investigation, it is difficult to determine whether bias arises from algorithm design or deliberate intervention. Companies can easily attribute such problems to a “technical glitch”! The Brazilian experience also highlighted the importance of combining three interconnected arenas of struggle: mass struggle on the ground, legal action to hold digital platforms accountable and regulate their operations, and organized digital activism. Mass mobilization in the streets was accompanied by legal challenges against Meta and the development of a wide-ranging digital campaign that used social media effectively to reach millions of voters. This experience shows that the digital left’s struggle cannot replace grassroots struggle. It can reinforce and complement it. This is where digital autonomy emerges as the fifth pillar of the left’s independence, alongside ideological, organizational, financial, and media autonomy. Genuine political independence is no longer possible without a meaningful degree of autonomy over digital tools, platforms, and infrastructure, the protection of data, and the capacity for mass communication and organization free from the monopolistic control of capitalist corporations and major powers. Digital autonomy does not mean withdrawing from digital platforms. It means using them today with a critical, progressive awareness while working to develop open-source, democratically-governed digital alternatives and to build and strengthen independent technical capacities within the left. A left that fails to develop its digital autonomy and technological tools will remain at the mercy of its class adversaries in one of the most important arenas of contemporary political and social struggle. Lessons for the left worldwide The Brazilian experience cannot be reproduced mechanically. Every society has its own conditions and balance of class and political forces. The Brazilian approach to building alliances and working together can nevertheless offer valuable lessons. The unity the left needs is neither a single party nor a centralized leadership imposing its vision on everyone. It is flexible, democratic cooperation among diverse forces, grounded in common programs, respect for autonomy and pluralism, and meaningful participation by the grassroots, young people, and women. Such cooperation can be developed locally, regionally, and globally through different left-wing fronts and alliances on the ground, as well as digital left networks and internationals that contribute to the exchange of experience, coordinate shared initiatives and struggles, and work toward progressive digital alternatives. Lula’s victory offers an experience worth studying and learning from. It demonstrates the possibility of cooperation among left-wing forces despite their differences, while recognizing the other factors that contributed to the result. The left does not need to erase its diversity to unite. It needs to turn that diversity into an organized and effective force, strengthen its independence across all five pillars, and pursue the struggle for freedom, equality, and social justice while developing democratic, humanist socialist alternatives to capitalism. Rezgar Akrawi is a leftist writer and researcher focused on technology, AI, the digital revolution, and the development of contemporary leftist thought and practice in response to these transformations. He works as an expert in systems development and e-governance and is a theorist of the concept of the “Digital Left .” This article was produced by Globetrotter .

articles.title: Western Sahara at a tipping point as US pushes for Moroccan ‘autonomy’ plan
articles.author: Nicholas Mwangi
articles.content: Large numbers of Sahrawi citizens took to the streets in El Aaiún , the largest city in Western Sahara, on Monday, to demand a just United Nations-sponsored solution that guarantees their right to freedom, self-determination, and independence. The demonstrations come as the United States allegedly pushes a draft UN Security Council resolution that would make Morocco’s autonomy plan the sole basis for negotiations over the future of the territory. The US-drafted text, reportedly circulated among Security Council members on October 22, has drawn strong objections from the Polisario Front, the Sahrawi independence movement, as well as human rights and solidarity organizations. Arguing the proposal risks predetermining the outcome of negotiations by placing Morocco’s plan over Western Sahara at the center of the process, rather than allowing the Sahrawi people to freely decide their political future. The dispute comes as the Security Council considers the future of the United Nations Mission for the Referendum in Western Sahara (MINURSO), established in 1991 to support the UN-OAU Settlement Plan, which included a referendum on self-determination. Polisario Front warns it could withdraw from the peace process In a letter from October 22 to Aglaia Balta, Greece’s permanent representative to the United Nations and current president of the Security Council, Dr Sidi Mohamed Omar, the Polisario Front’s representative to the UN, strongly rejected the US zero-draft. Omar said the text “fully reflects the national position of the penholder as well as that of Morocco, the occupying state,” describing it as “another extremely dangerous, unprecedented departure” from international law and the UN framework governing Western Sahara’s decolonization. He added that the process cannot be reduced to Security Council Resolution 2797 (2025), but must be understood within the wider body of relevant UN resolutions and the original agreement underpinning MINURSO. The mission was established under Resolution 690 (1991), following an agreement between the Polisario Front and Morocco, based on the UN-OAU Settlement Plan. According to the Polisario Front, changing the framework unilaterally would align the mission with Morocco’s position and undermine international efforts to resolve the territory’s status through decolonization. “The non-compliance of Morocco, the occupying state, with its commitments under the UN-OAU Settlement Plan, which was adopted unanimously by the Security Council, cannot justify any infringement upon the inalienable right of the Sahrawi people to self-determination and sovereignty over their homeland,” Omar wrote. Emphasizing that the text “cannot constitute a basis for any deliberations on MINURSO or the peace process in Western Sahara” and warned that, if it passed without “substantive and meaningful changes,” the movement “would have no choice but to disengage from the peace process as a whole.” But remains committed to a just, lasting, and definitive peace. Morocco’s autonomy plan One of the main concerns raised by the Western Sahara Research Watch (WSRW) is the reported change in the language of the draft. The text reportedly describes Morocco’s autonomy proposal as the “only basis” for negotiations, strengthening the language of the 2025 resolution, which referred to it as “a basis.” The WSRW argues that the difference is substantial. While autonomy could theoretically be one option freely chosen by the Sahrawi people, making Morocco’s proposal the sole basis in advance risks narrowing the political choices available to them. The organization asks, “How can the people freely determine the territory’s future if negotiations may only take place within a model that presupposes Moroccan sovereignty?” Going farther, the draft describes autonomy under Moroccan sovereignty as the most feasible solution. This shifts the purpose of negotiations away from determining Western Sahara’s status and towards negotiating the terms of Moroccan control. The WSRW also warns that the draft’s references to consulting Sahrawis in the territory, in refugee camps, and throughout the diaspora do not guarantee that they will have a decisive role in determining the outcome. “Being heard is not the same as being allowed to decide,” the organization argues. The European Association of Lawyers for Democracy and World Human Rights (ELDH ) has also called on the United Nations to uphold international law and the Sahrawi people’s right to self-determination. International law and the question of sovereignty The Campaign for the Right to Self-Determination of the People of Western Sahara (CODESA) has also rejected the premise that international recognition of Morocco’s claim can determine the territory’s legal status. “Recognition by third states cannot turn occupation into sovereignty,” the organization argues. Western Sahara remains on the UN list of Non-Self-Governing Territories. In its 1975 advisory opinion, the International Court of Justice found that the materials and information presented to it did not establish any tie of territorial sovereignty between Western Sahara and Morocco that would displace the application of self-determination through the free and genuine expression of the territory’s people. CODESA also points to the UN General Assembly Resolution 34/37, adopted in 1979, which deplored Morocco’s continued occupation of Western Sahara and reaffirmed the right of the Sahrawi people to self-determination and independence. It further cites the UN Legal Counsel’s 2002 opinion on the legality of resource exploration in the territory and the 2024 rulings of the Court of Justice of the European Union, reaffirming Western Sahara’s separate and distinct status from Morocco. CODESA maintains that a political outcome cannot be declared in advance and then presented as self-determination. It invokes UN General Assembly Resolution 1541 (XV), which sets out principles relevant to the exercise of self-determination, including that integration with another state must result from the freely expressed wishes of the people through an informed and democratic process. The organization also objects to the United States’ prominent role as facilitator, arguing that a mediator that has already recognized Morocco’s claim cannot be assumed to be impartial. It maintains that negotiations must allow the parties to present their positions without imposing one party’s proposal as the only acceptable framework. “Negotiations in which only the occupying power’s proposal may be discussed are not negotiations; they are terms of surrender offered to the occupied people,” CODESA says. Over the years, Morocco’s autonomy plan for Western Sahara has gained diplomatic support as several countries have shifted their positions towards recognizing Moroccan sovereignty over the disputed territory rewarded by trade deals. But these diplomatic changes have not resolved the central question of Western Sahara’s future, and the right of the Sahrawi people to determine their own political status.

articles.title: Dockworkers at 110 ports worldwide strike against war and genocide
articles.author: Ana Vračar
articles.content: Dockworkers across five continents and more than 110 ports launched a second historic international day of action against militarization and genocide on October 30. “We no longer want to work for war nor to pay for it,” José Nivoi of the Autonomous Collective of Port Workers (Coordinamento Autonomo Lavoratori Portuali, CALP) in Genoa said as actions kicked off. “Because the conditions we’re experiencing in Italy today, they’re the same conditions being experienced on five different continents.” Ports must serve life, not destruction The port workers’ actions are grounded in the Istanbul Declaration adopted earlier this year, which analyzes the impact of the growing arms transports on work in harbors worldwide. In the declaration and the interventions that followed, dockworkers outlined how this trend comes hand in hand with the erosion of working conditions, including the contractualization of work and aggressive austerity cuts. Friday’s actions are supported by roughly 25 unions from Australia to the United States and Uruguay, and from India to Mexico. A notable cluster of ports is located across the Mediterranean, where the first day of action – held in February this year – was launched. The dockworkers’ union ENEDEP led the strike call in Greece, receiving support from education workers and school children. Source: PAME International/Flickr Over the past months, dockworkers from Italy, the Basque Country, Turkey, Greece , and Morocco were joined by others. The expanded list added organizations from Croatia, Cyprus, Denmark, France, Germany, Ireland , Montenegro, the Netherlands, Portugal, Slovenia, Spain, and Sweden. “Our message is clear: dockworkers don’t work for war,” the Moroccan Democratic Labor Organization (Organisation Démocratique du Travail, ODT) from Tangiers port said at a press conference in late October. “Ports must serve life, transporting food and medicines that sustain our communities. They must be places of cooperation between peoples, never instruments of destruction.” No harbor for genocide A notable emphasis throughout the day is dockworkers’ solidarity with Palestine, including expressions of support from the Boycott, Divestment and Sanctions (BDS) movement and the Global Sumud Flotilla . “With over 90% of Israeli imports arriving by sea, ports around the world are the chokepoint of Israel’s apartheid economy,” BDS and other organizations wrote on social media. “On October 30, dockworkers will show that, together, we can break the chain supplying Israel’s genocide, apartheid and occupation.” While the role of Mediterranean ports in fueling the genocide in Gaza has been more publicly exposed, the role of harbors in other regions remains perhaps less visible. That is precisely why the participation of dockworkers from Asia in the second international day of action is so significant. Read more: Indian port workers refuse to handle military cargo bound for Israel “In the last year, India’s major ports have been conduits from Indian public and private sector companies exporting to Israel’s Elbit Systems factories in Yokneam and Ramat Hasharon,” BDS and others wrote . “These factories manufacture artillery, munitions and ammunitions that has been documented to have been used in the genocide in Gaza.” “We firmly believe that support for Palestine should be channeled through our states, because today Israel enjoys a level of international impunity that allows it to carry out a genocide,” Nivoi said on Friday. “Therefore, we emphasize today that people must mobilize – not only in response to the rising cost of living, but above all to definitively liberate Palestine from Zionism.” Dockworkers’ action converges into general strike in Italy Italy and Genoa in particular have been a key node for building trade union solidarity with Palestine since 2023. Conscious of the links between growing militarization, imperialist drives around the world, and hardening austerity in Italy, CALP and the grassroots union Unione Sindacale di Base (USB) also called for a convergence of local movements – leading to a new general strike . According to early estimates , approximately 2 million people in Italy responded to this call, including many students and young people. Over the past weeks, as students in several European countries took to the streets, youth groups across Italy have also been demonstrating against cuts to essential services. Read more: Italian government to deploy troops to Milan after anti-austerity protests On Friday, these groups promptly responded to the general strike call. “The student-worker alliance is growing ever stronger: across the country, students and young people are mobilizing – through occupations, encampments, assemblies, and demonstrations – against the government, while also promoting the upcoming general strike,” Marta Collot from the left party Potere al Popolo emphasized ahead of the day of action. “Labor can stop war” While witnessing the continuity of dockworkers’ actions in one part of the world brings much inspiration, trade unionists involved in preparing the day also emphasized the significance of the initiative expanding. Not all organizations were in a position to launch a strike, but they still recognized the importance of sending an anti-militarist message from their docks. In a comment for BreakThrough News , trade unionists from the Port of Vukovar, Croatia – mapped alongside unions taking part in the day of action – stressed the importance of dockworkers’ anti-war campaigning. Their point was concrete: wars fought elsewhere reshape livelihoods, shipping routes, and working conditions at home. Dockworkers in Koper, Slovenia, were among those joining the dockworkers’ second international day of action. Source: SŽPD/Facebook Yet the struggle is not only for dockworkers to fight, European trade unionists insist. As USB’s Francesco Staccioli pointed out in late October, the struggle against war remains a wider struggle for workers’ rights and social justice. Because of this, he emphasized, October 30 should be taken as a starting point to widen the scope of action further. “Labor can stop war. It can stop the genocide of the Palestinian people. It can stop imperialist aggression,” he said.

articles.title: One year after the election killings, Tanzania still awaits justice
articles.author: Nicholas Mwangi
articles.content: One year ago, Tanzanians went to the polls in an election followed by deadly protests and a violent security crackdown. The immediate unrest has since subsided, but the wounds remain, and the demand for justice continues. President Samia Suluhu Hassan was declared the winner with 97.66% of the vote, an overwhelming margin that came with the exclusion of opposition forces and mounting restrictions on political activities. The disputed election and the violence that followed exposed deep tensions over Tanzania’s political realities, democratic participation, and the state’s response to dissent. A year on, not a single official has been held responsible, and justice for the victims and their families remains out of reach. A disputed election and a deadly crackdown The violence of October 2025 did not erupt out of nowhere. In the months before the election , opposition parties faced mounting restrictions, rallies were disrupted, and political activists were arrested. Opposition leader Tundu Lissu was arrested in April 2025 and charged with treason, which kept him out of the electoral process. His party, CHADEMA, was then excluded from the election after refusing to sign the electoral code of ethics. These developments narrowed the space for political competition and raised serious questions about the credibility of the vote. When Tanzanians went to the polls on October 29, demonstrations broke out in several parts of the country, including Dar es Salaam, Arusha, and Mwanza. Protesters rejected the election and demanded political change. The government responded with a nationwide curfew and an internet shutdown that lasted several days, cutting off communication and the flow of information as security forces confronted demonstrators. Human rights organizations documented the use of lethal force against protesters and other people who did not pose an imminent threat to life. The scale of the killings became clearer in April 2026, when a government-appointed Commission of Inquiry reported that at least 518 people had died during the election-related violence. Thousands were also injured. The opposition has maintained that the death toll was higher, with concerns also raised about people who remain missing and the circumstances in which bodies were removed from hospitals and mortuaries. The commission submitted its report to President Samia Suluhu Hassan on April 23. However, the full report has not been made public, leaving victims’ families and the wider public without access to the complete findings. One year later, impunity remains On October 28, Amnesty International marked the anniversary by condemning the continuing failure to hold officials accountable for the violence. “Not a single official has been criminally investigated, let alone prosecuted and punished for the excessive force that Tanzanian security forces used against protesters,” said Tigere Chagutah, Amnesty International’s Regional Director for East and Southern Africa. The organization also warned that, instead of opening a transparent accountability process, the authorities had increasingly used counterterrorism laws against opposition supporters and government critics. The withholding of the inquiry report has become a central obstacle to establishing the truth. Without public access to the findings, it remains difficult to scrutinize the evidence, understand the circumstances surrounding individual deaths, and determine what action the government intends to take against those responsible. President Samia Suluhu Hassan and other government officials have repeatedly portrayed the protests as a foreign-backed attempt to overthrow the government, a coordinated plot to destabilize the country. Activists argue that this narrative serves to deflect responsibility, evade justice, and excuse the authorities’ slow response to the killings. Tanzania today is marked by silence, not reconciliation. And a nation cannot simply move on from an atrocity of this scale without truth and accountability.

articles.title: Dolores Huerta, Legendary Farmworker Organizer & Activist, Dies at 96
articles.content: This is a rush transcript. Copy may not be in its final form. AMY GOODMAN : This is Democracy Now! , democracynow.org, The War and Peace Report . I’m Amy Goodman. The legendary labor organizer, feminist and civil rights activist Dolores Huerta has died at the age of 96. She was co-founder of the National Farm Workers Association in 1962 and then the United Farm Workers of America. She worked with Cesar Chavez at both groups. The United Farm Workers grew out of a merger between the National Farm Workers Association and the Filipino-led Agricultural Workers Organizing Committee. Dolores Huerta coined the phrase ” ¡Sí se puede! ,” “Yes, we can!” It became a rallying cry for farmworkers, a lasting slogan for social justice movements. Dolores Huerta appeared on Democracy Now! many times. We’ll hear her in her own words later in the broadcast, but first let’s turn to the trailer of the 2017 documentary Dolores , which featured interviews with Angela Davis, Gloria Steinem, Hillary Clinton and Nancy Pelosi. SPEAKER NANCY PELOSI : Dolores is an icon. CURTIS ACOSTA : She’s a civil rights hero. CESAR CHAVEZ : She’s the first general that I followed into war. HILLARY CLINTON : She’s not afraid to speak truth to power. ROBERT F. KENNEDY : Dolores Huerta, who is an old friend of mine. ANGELA DAVIS : The FBI knew how dangerous Dolores was. Dolores came up with the slogan ¡Sí se puede! SEN . BARACK OBAMA : Yes, we can. INTERVIEWER : You were a young girl growing up in America in the ’40s. You must have had a dream. DOLORES HUERTA : After I had seen the miserable conditions of farmworkers, Cesar Chavez said, “We have to organize a union.” You had this ambiance all around you that you could really change the world. REPORTER : It’s, beyond question, the largest gathering on behalf of farmworkers in California history. PROTESTER : I wish they all go back to where they came from. We have no labor trouble troubles. UNIDENTIFIED : She wasn’t asking for permission. She just did what needed to be done. ELISEO MEDINA : She has such a firm belief in what she’s doing — DOLORES HUERTA : We’re never giving up. ELISEO MEDINA : — that she infects you with it. Dolores Huerta. DOLORES HUERTA : Ninety thousand people were poisoned in the fields of the United States of America. RANDY SHAW : The farmworkers founded the whole idea of environmental justice. UNIDENTIFIED : Men were threatened by her power. UNIDENTIFIED : She’s a very volatile individual. UNIDENTIFIED : She’s an insult. UNIDENTIFIED : People wanted to see her in a more traditional role. DOLORES HUERTA : I left a couple of my children behind. MARIA ELENA CHAVEZ : That’s part of the sacrifice that we made and that we had to make. DOLORES HUERTA : And it still pains me when I think about it. CURTIS ACOSTA : People in power have no idea of the true heroes of this country. GLORIA STEINEM : I would not have been able to see what’s hidden in the fields of our country without Dolores. CURTIS ACOSTA : We’re knee deep in sexism when it comes to why she isn’t studied and why people don’t know her. UNIDENTIFIED : Latina girls need to see statues of you. JUANITA CHÁVEZ: We were trying to set the record straight. I mean, women cannot be written out of history. DOLORES HUERTA : Down with violence! ¡Abajo! Down with racism! ¡Abajo! Down with sexism! ¡Abajo! AMY GOODMAN : The trailer to the documentary Dolores , directed by Peter Bratt. We’re joined now by Maria Hinojosa, the Pulitzer Prize-winning journalist and founder of Futuro Media, host of Latino USA . Maria, you have covered Dolores Huerta for decades. Just last year, you interviewed her for — after a New York Times investigation exposed the sexual abuse and rape allegations against the UFW co-founder Cesar Chavez. Dolores Huerta herself publicly disclosed that Chavez had raped her decades earlier. You talked to her about that, and we’ll talk about that later. But first, let’s talk about Dolores Huerta’s legacy. Who was Dolores Huerta, born in 1930, died at the age of 96? MARIA HINOJOSA : She was a fighter. She also — Amy, one of the things that I love talking about is Dolores was not only a labor organizer, a civil rights organizer, a feminist, committed, always optimistic about the possibilities of this country, but she loved life. And I want people to remember that. Like, when I would be with Dolores, and it would be kind of wrapping up a night of being out doing an event, and I’d be like, “Well, I’m going to the hotel. I’m going to sleep,” she’s like, “Really? We’re going to go out. We’re going to go out and go dancing. We’re going to listen to music.” And I’m like, “What?” And she’s like — this was Dolores. And I think it’s important to remember that as much as she fought for people, the most vulnerable, she also fought to love life and to love her kids, her kids, her grandkids, her great-grandkids, great-great-grandkids, still here. So, I don’t know. She was always so optimistic. Like, when I would ask her, “Things are looking bad,” she’s always like, “There’s always an opportunity to organize and make things better.” And I’m like, “OK, Dolores, let’s keep it like that: positive.” AMY GOODMAN : So, let’s hear Dolores Huerta in her own words. In 2017, she came into our studio to talk about her life and the documentary that had just been named about her, Dolores . She talked about her childhood. DOLORES HUERTA : Well, I was born in the state of New Mexico and moved to Stockton when I was 6 years old. My parents divorced, and my mother took us to Stockton. And that’s where I was raised, and that’s where I started my initial organizing, in that area. AMY GOODMAN : And how did you, as a teenager, decide that organizing was going to be the path of your life, and specifically working with farmworkers? DOLORES HUERTA : Well, that was kind of accidental, as where I grew up, Stockton, California, is an agricultural community. And as a youngster, I was a Girl Scout for 10 years of my life, and I was in a lot of different social clubs. But when I met Mr. Ross and he showed us what we could actually do by coming together and organizing and taking direct nonviolent action, then I was really — I thought, “Oh my goodness! This is what I want to do with my life.” And so, I became a schoolteacher, then I left teaching to go to Delano to start the union there. AMY GOODMAN : And farmworkers themselves, the grape boycott that you helped to lead, the worker strikes, talk about how you organized them. What was the strategy? And then talk about your response to the impact that it had. DOLORES HUERTA : Well, the thing is that when people think about the strike and the — it’s very dramatic, colorful. But what they don’t see is like the three years before the strike, where we organize workers in house meetings. And this is the method that Fred Ross taught us, by meeting in people’s homes, you know, one family at a time, and then bringing them all together. And this is the same kind of a method that we use today with my foundation, the Dolores Huerta Foundation, where we’re working on ending the school-to-prison pipeline, working on environmental issues, on economic issues and, you know, inspiring people that they — and motivating them that they have power, but that they can make the changes, but that they have to make the changes. No one can do it for them. And this is the kind of work that we do, using that same organizing method, one family at a time, one family at a time. And it’s very tedious, and it’s very time-consuming, but then the results are really wonderful. We recently settled a lawsuit with our current high school district in California, in Bakersfield, for the expulsion and suspension of African American and Latino students. And now they have to change their policies, and they have to change their procedures, to keep the students in school. And so, we’ll go out there, and we organize the parents, and then the parents are the ones that take on the — they become the leaders of making sure that some of these policies are changed. AMY GOODMAN : When was the grape boycott? DOLORES HUERTA : It was in 1968. We started the boycott in 1968. AMY GOODMAN : And explain what it was. What was the strategy you took? DOLORES HUERTA : Well, the strategy was that we had farmworkers come out from California, and again using those same methods of meeting people in their homes and organizing groups throughout the United States and asking people to come and support, number one, to get people to picket the stores and ask people not to buy grapes. And at the end of the day, we had like 17 million people that were not eating grapes. And this is what brought the growers to the bargaining table. AMY GOODMAN : What about Robert Kennedy’s role? How significant was it? And how did you and Cesar Chavez reach out to him? DOLORES HUERTA : Well, Senator Kennedy had been a supporter early on. He came to California. He had a hearing right in the middle of the strike. And there’s a very dramatic moment in the movie, Dolores , where Robert Kennedy tells the sheriff of Kern County and the district attorney to read the Constitution of the United States, because they were continuously arresting us, and so that we wouldn’t be — you know, we wouldn’t be able to picket. And so, he was a great supporter. And then, of course, we helped him very much in his campaign, when he was running for the presidency, by going out there and getting people out to vote. AMY GOODMAN : I wanted to turn to a clip of your film, Dolores . AUDIENCE : ¡Sí se puede! ARTURO RODRIGUEZ : ¡Sí se puede! AUDIENCE : ¡Sí se puede! ARTURO RODRIGUEZ : For Cesar, ” ¡Sí se puede! ” wasn’t just a slogan. DOLORES HUERTA : When people in Arizona said — they told me, “No, Dolores, no se puede . You can’t do this in Arizona. Only in California,” my response to them was ” ¡Sí se puede! ” ¡Sí se puede! ¡Sí se puede! MICHELLE MILLER : Hers was the rallying cry that would later come to define the presidential campaign of candidate Barack Obama. SEN . BARACK OBAMA : Yes, we can. ORGANIZER : Have you heard President Obama say, “Yes, we can”? It came from Cesar Chavez: ” ¡Sí se puede! ” ANGELA DAVIS : Dolores Huerta came up with the slogan ” ¡Sí se puede! ” And we all attribute that to Cesar Chavez, even Barack Obama. Of course, when he gave her the Presidential Medal of Freedom, he had to correct himself. PRESIDENT BARACK OBAMA : On a personal note, Dolores was very gracious when I told her I had stolen her slogan, ” ¡Sí se puede! Yes, we can!” Knowing her, I’m pleased that she let me off easy, because Dolores does not play. AMY GOODMAN : That was a clip from the documentary Dolores . So, ” ¡Sí se puede! ” was your phrase. DOLORES HUERTA : Mm-hmm, yes. AMY GOODMAN : When did you come up with it? DOLORES HUERTA : In Arizona, actually, in 1972, when Cesar was fasting, was doing a 25-day water-only fast, kind of to take the hatred out of the hearts of the growers. That’s the way that he put it. And so, we were trying to organize people to come and to join us, and speaking to a group of professional Latinos, asking them to come and join us. And they said, “No, you can’t do this in Arizona. Only in California. No se puede . No, you can’t.” And my response to them was “Yes, we can. ¡Sí se puede! , in Arizona, the way that we organized in California.” AMY GOODMAN : I wanted to turn to another clip of the film that’s now out in theaters around the country. This is Dolores , and the clip begins with the feminist icon Gloria Steinem. GLORIA STEINEM : I didn’t really know Dolores before New York. But I think I was scared of her. I don’t think that Dolores thought I was worth the trouble, until I got Huntington Hartford to picket the A&P, which of course got press, because the heir to the A&P fortune was boycotting the A&P. After that, we became partners. EMILIO HUERTA : My mother was raised a Catholic and very traditional. And prior to going to New York City, she really didn’t speak of feminism. DOLORES HUERTA : I was in New York when the feminist movement was being born. But my mind was focused on getting all of those women at those conventions to support the farmworkers. ANGELA DAVIS : There was a time when rarely could you discover women of color who would identify as feminists, because it was assumed to be a question simply of gender. And if it was a question simply of gender, that gender was white. GLORIA STEINEM : When social justice movements arise in a patriarchal system, all kinds of false divisions are made. AMY GOODMAN : So, that was Angela Davis and Gloria Steinem talking about Dolores. That’s Dolores Huerta. And the new film about her, that’s a clip. You are often seen in photographs with, oh, all your male colleagues. Can you talk about when you came to see the importance of the intersectionality of the labor movement, the women’s movement, people of color and the feminist movement? DOLORES HUERTA : Well, in order to be able to win, through the boycott, to begin with, we had to reach out to all of the different organizations, and, otherwise, we could not win. I mean, the 17 million Americans that stopped eating grapes, you know, included all of these different organizations. And so — and I think that’s one of the messages that we have today, is that, you know, the only way that we’re going to be able to, again, counter the Trump administration is that we’ve all got to work together. You know, we’ve all got to work on the environmental issues. We’ve all got to support labor unions. We’ve got to support the immigrant rights movement, etc., and the LGBT movement also, because we can’t be in our silos and win. We’ve all got to work together. I think that’s the lesson that we have. AMY GOODMAN : That was Dolores Huerta speaking here in our studio in 2017 as we played clips from the documentary that year, Dolores . Dolores Huerta died Wednesday at the age of 96. As she talked about supporting all the different communities, Maria Hinojosa, she actually evolved in her views on those communities, and even what she called herself. MARIA HINOJOSA : And I think that this is one of the great lessons from Dolores Huerta, is that she was very public about the fact that she evolved. So, for example, she did not like calling herself a feminist at first. So, Gloria Steinem says, “I was afraid of Dolores.” I think Dolores was like, “Well, you’re a white feminist. I’m not sure I identify with you.” And then Dolores became a feminist icon and spoke about her feminism, which was really important for so many Latinas in this country and around Latin America. Dolores, on the question of reproductive rights, was at first distant. The question of abortion was not her issue. And then she evolved, and she became a huge supporter of reproductive rights and the struggle for reproductive rights. And on the question of LGBTQ issues, again, at first she was a little bit distant, and then, in her own family, it turned out that she had a queer daughter. And this turned out to be a real interesting conversation with her. So, I think one of the lessons from Dolores is we can evolve, and we can talk about the fact that we evolve. And that’s why, I mean, I think it’s kind of wonderful, Amy, that you and I did not get on the phone before we did this interview, but we’re both wearing the colors of Dolores Huerta: red and black. AMY GOODMAN : I wanted to go to a very difficult time in her life, and this is when we last spoke to you, Maria. It was actually just this past year. Talk about the New York Times investigation into her longtime co-organizer Cesar Chavez and what was revealed. MARIA HINOJOSA : Right. So, in March of this year, a big story breaks in The New York Times that says Cesar Chavez had raped Dolores Huerta at least once and that Cesar Chavez had been abusing sexually many people, many women, within the farmworker movement. This was devastating for Dolores Huerta. I was actually flying back from Mexico City that morning, and we got the call that she wanted to speak to me first, before she spoke to any other journalist. So, you can imagine, Amy, just kind of the weight of Dolores Huerta saying, “I want to speak to you.” It was such a difficult interview, because, again, Dolores was the perennial optimist organizer, always happy to do anything, 'til all hours. And on this interview, when I sat down in the studio, I said, “Dolores, can we go on camera?” She said, “No.” She said, “I've been reading The New York Times report just this morning. You don’t want to see how I look today.” She was devastated. She said, “I’ve been crying all morning.” And the thing is, Amy, you can imagine being 96 years old and having to talk about the fact that she was raped at least once. Interestingly, when I did the first interview, she was prepared to accept that she had been raped once. The second time, she said, “Well, Cesar forced me to have sex.” And I was like, “Dolores, that’s rape.” The second interview, 24 hours later, with John Quiñones, that’s when she said, “Actually, I was raped twice.” This was so hard for her to admit that, like me, she was now a survivor of rape, and that this was another — another group that she had to identify with. It was devastating. AMY GOODMAN : Let’s turn to that interview you did with Dolores Huerta earlier this year, speaking about why she continued to stand with Cesar Chavez after he had raped her. DOLORES HUERTA : Well, I think the only way that I can explain it is when we have to look at the sea of all of the things that we accomplished for farmworkers, you know, the fact that they have the basic human needs when they’re working, you know, the things that they were deprived of, you know, the bathrooms, the drinking water, the rest periods, you know, to be treated as decent human beings out there in the fields. And we’re talking about millions of farmworkers. And I think my staying quiet and not revealing this, I don’t know if that contributed or didn’t contribute, but in my mind, when people say, “Why didn’t you — why didn’t you leave? Why didn’t you tell people?” well, this is why, because I felt that my coming out and saying what occurred would hurt the movement. AMY GOODMAN : And I want to go to another clip of, Maria, your interview with Dolores Huerta. MARIA HINOJOSA : Are you concerned that people will say, “How is it possible that the brilliant Dolores Huerta no se dio cuenta , that she didn’t realize?” Are you concerned that you’re going to have to answer that question? DOLORES HUERTA : Well, I think that’s pretty common. I think that women, when they do come forward with their stories, instead of getting the kind of support that they need, they get attacked, or they’re not believed. And we’ve seen this happen throughout history. We’ll just have to deal with that if it does happen. Hopefully it won’t. But if it does, we’ll just have to deal with it. And the workers know that they are no longer alone. AMY GOODMAN : That was Dolores Huerta revealing, in this very painful discussion after The New York Times exposé of Cesar Chavez raping and sexually assaulting women. She said it happened to her, as well. In fact, two of her children. MARIA HINOJOSA : See, you’re not going to believe this. I know you believe it, because you know that you and I only deal with fact. Yesterday morning, at about this time, I was coming up with a list of stories that I wanted to pitch to my team, because we have a pitch meeting today. And on my little Post-it, because I’m a Post-it girl, I had written “DH part two.” I wanted to ask Dolores — today — if I could do another interview with her, a follow-up interview with her. The revelations broke in March. It was now at the end of the year. Would she speak again about what happened and how she felt about it? Look, Dolores Huerta, she did sacrifice this for el pueblo , for la raza , for the cause. But I think we have to remember: If Dolores Huerta would have come out publicly at any time, I think people would have discredited her. People really held Cesar Chavez in this kind of high position. By the way, I was not a fan of Cesar Chavez. After in the early ’90s, I was like, “I have some questions about Cesar Chavez.” She defended him up until the end. Even when these revelations had come out, she had a hard time saying Cesar Chavez was a horrible person, because she admired him so much. AMY GOODMAN : I wanted to talk about her activism right through. I mean, she died at the age of 96. This is Dolores in her own words almost exactly a year ago. And let me be clear on this: We asked her if she would come on live. She’s 95 years old, and the show, for her, is at 5:00 in the morning. She said, “Absolutely.” This is Dolores talking about her activism. AMY GOODMAN : Can you talk about ICE targeting day labor centers in Los Angeles, for example, the Van Nuys center being raided 14 times since June, the focus on labor, on workers who are out at work when they are taken? DOLORES HUERTA : Yes, not only farmworkers, but we know our hospitality workers that work in our hotels, people who are laborers that work on construction sites. I mean, absolutely no one is safe. If you happen to be just anybody on the street that happens to be a person that looks Latino or Asian or Black, you are subjected to the kidnapping and all of these tortures. And as we know, people have already been killed. You know, this is the kind of horrific, horrific terrorism that the Latino and the people of color community are now living. And God knows that it has to stop. AMY GOODMAN : So, that was Dolores Huerta last year, during President Trump’s second term, taking on ICE , Maria. MARIA HINOJOSA : So, the thing — there are so many lessons from Dolores Huerta. And I would often turn to her and just, you know, just feel desperation about our country, and she would always say, “You have to remember people power.” And I’m like, “What are you talking about?” She was like, “What the United Farm Workers did was to organize the most vulnerable, invisible people and actually win the strike, win on so many levels.” And so, this notion of people power, she was like, “It’s unstoppable.” But it’s not people power on Instagram or on X or on social media. It was people power putting their bodies into the streets to protest and to care for others. So, it’s no surprise that Dolores Huerta would say, “I’m absolutely going to come on at 5:00 in the morning to talk about this.” AMY GOODMAN : And just as we wrap up, she, of course, talked about her support for RFK , for Robert F. Kennedy, and his activism supporting the farmworkers. She was there at the Ambassador Hotel when he was assassinated? MARIA HINOJOSA : And when I asked her about that, I was like, “Dolores, you know, you’ve been part of history. You were there when RFK was shot.” And her response, Amy, was, honestly, shocking to me. She said, “I carried so much weight and sadness about that. I felt like I should have done something more.” And I’m like, “What are you talking about?” She was like, “I should have protected him more. I feel” — like, she carried the weight. I was like, “What? Did you want to stand in front of the bullet?” But that was Dolores, always thinking of others, always thinking of the movement, not thinking about herself. And yet, she was a deeply emotional human being who carried these emotions. So, knowing that she was sad that she wasn’t able to save RFK’s life was profound, like many of the lessons of Dolores Huerta, so profound. AMY GOODMAN : Maria Hinojosa, Pulitzer Prize-winning journalist, founder of Futuro Media. She’s the host of Latino USA . We’ll link to all of our interviews with Dolores Huerta and also Maria’s interview with Dolores Huerta earlier this year. Go to democracynow.org. Coming up, we speak to Sofia Liguori, a research engineer who resigned from Google’s AI unit DeepMind over the company’s work with the U.S. and Israeli military. Stay with us. [break] AMY GOODMAN : Alice Gerrard and band singing “When I Loved You” at the Brooklyn [Folk] Festival.

articles.title: How the UAE is fueling Sudan’s catastrophic war
articles.author: Zoe Alexandra
articles.content: Sudan’s “civil war” is a proxy war for gold, now waged from above with foreign-armed drones. Journalist and researcher Mosaab Baba says Sudan’s “gold curse” has both the army and the UAE-backed Rapid Support Forces (RSF) increasingly striking civilian targets in a neocolonial war entering its fourth year, which has already killed thousands of civilians and left millions facing famine. With most of Sudan’s gold now funneled to Abu Dhabi, Baba tells Rania Khalek and Zoe Alexandra the country has become a “backyard” for the UAE, Egypt, Saudi Arabia and Turkey to extract precious minerals, farmland and access to the Red Sea. A year after the fall of El Fasher, he also explains why the world’s largest humanitarian crisis keeps slipping out of the headlines. Baba also unpacks how the legacy of the December Revolution still offers hope for a sovereign, people-led Sudan, and lays out the stakes driving the Sudanese campaign against Emirati diplomat Lana Nusseibeh’s potential bid to become the next UN secretary-general. “The only glimmer of hope is that Sudanese people themselves are starting to realize how insane this war is [and] how much they need to remove these neocolonial leaders from the country.” Watch full episodes of BT Live, join breakthroughnews.org as a member today! ****** Rough transcript follows: [Speaker 1:] The UAE is the main culprit in pushing for the RSF to take over Sudan, driven by the gold trade and regional domination. They’re closely allied with the Ethiopian government, and unfortunately, Abiy Ahmed is aligned with them, though not fully carrying out their wishes. They have a strong influence on Chad and are the biggest investors in Egypt. This is why we explain this as a neo-colonial war. These powers might support both sides but have no issues with each other. [Speaker 2:] Moving on to Sudan, another drone strike occurred this week, blamed on the Sudanese army, killing dozens in a crowded market in Nala. The RSF’s de facto capital in Darfur was affected, and RSF drones knocked out power across central and eastern Sudan, including Khartoum. Sudanese journalist and researcher Mossab Baba joins us to discuss this proxy war, now in its fourth year, and the foreign-supplied weapons that have killed thousands of civilians. [Speaker 3:] Thank you for having me. I appreciate it. [Speaker 2:] We appreciate your time and analysis. Let’s start with the latest in Nala. Local tolls range from 21 to over a hundred killed. The army claims it’s softening RSF positions ahead of a ground assault. This follows hundreds killed in drone strikes last week. Is this recent strike the opening of a push into Darfur? [Speaker 3:] There have been changes in how both sides conduct this war, with drone strikes becoming more prominent. It shifted from relying on mortars and ground forces to drone strikes over the last year and a half. The pattern is unusual; whenever there’s stagnation between the forces, drones start firing. The SAF targets markets, as seen in Nala and a disputed area between Sudan and South Sudan. After these attacks, the RSF retaliates by hitting civilian infrastructure in SAF areas, leaving millions without power. The strikes in Nala were fatal, and similar incidents have occurred before, like in West Darfur. This shift to drone warfare is partly due to the increasing international drone market, with both sides having partners willing to supply weapons. The SAF, as the official army, faces fewer issues bringing in weapons, but the RSF relies on a network traced by a UN report, mainly through Libya and Chad. [Speaker 2:] The Sudanese citizen is being pummeled by this war, and neither side takes responsibility. The SAF doesn’t acknowledge strikes hitting civilians, and the RSF remains silent on their attacks. This leads to speculation about rogue elements within these camps. The SAF camp is fragmented, with different factions and militias, while the RSF has rogue elements crossing borders. [Speaker 3:] The use of drones is a dangerous escalation in this war, now over three years old, causing one of the worst humanitarian catastrophes. International players are involved on both sides. This isn’t merely a Sudanese conflict. Powers like the UAE, Egypt, Turkey, and Saudi Arabia are involved. How did Sudan become a battleground for these powers? [Speaker 3:] The SAF and RSF were part of the same government under an imperial order. Decisions about Sudan go through Cairo, Abu Dhabi, and Riyadh. This control carries over from the Bashir regime, which handed Sudan to Gulf countries. Both SAF and RSF were recruited for the war in Yemen in 2015 and remain there. The war’s goal was to kill the people’s movement calling for sovereignty and wealth redistribution. The West views these demands as socialism, though in Sudan, it’s seen as government responsibility. Forcing Sudan to sign the Abraham Accords is another factor. Netanyahu often includes Sudan in his maps of the new Middle East. This is a late-stage neo-colonial order, with military forces lacking loyalty to the Sudanese people, allowing countries like Turkey, the UAE, Egypt, and Saudi Arabia to exploit Sudan for resources like gold and farmland. [Speaker 2:] Speaking of resources, what’s up for grabs in Sudan? Gold, farmland, Red Sea access—what are foreign powers targeting? [Speaker 3:] Gold is the most fatal, with the RSF utilizing it economically. Most gold ends up in the UAE, which has destabilized regions for gold mines. This gold rush causes instability, similar to the oil curse. Livestock is a close second, while agriculture struggles due to sustainability issues and food crises. Gold is a quick fix for militias and warlords running the economy and war. [Speaker 2:] It’s been one year since the ethnic cleansing in Al-Fashir, and several massacres have occurred since. Why hasn’t Sudan registered more on people’s radars? What international efforts are being made to end the conflict, and who’s stopping them? [Speaker 3:] Internally, there are efforts for national dialogue and a negotiated end to the war. Political parties and traditional leadership engage in people-to-people dialogue. Activists, especially in the diaspora, campaign against the UAE, which lobbies the UN and influences US policy. The UAE’s deep pockets are the main reason this conflict lacks attention. They’re pushing for the RSF to take over Sudan for gold trade and regional domination. [Speaker 2:] Eight years ago, the Sudanese revolution began, a hopeful moment for organizing across sectors. Now, the military establishment has co-opted and crushed it. Your thoughts on this? [Speaker 3:] The December revolution was a historic moment, uniting Sudan against the Bashir government. It was coerced by leadership and countries pressuring the military. Protests in Khartoum last December remembered the revolution. Many volunteers and activists emerged from it, maintaining social fabric and aid efforts. The revolution’s core discourse remains valid, and though affected by war, it will manifest differently as people realize the war’s insanity. [Speaker 2:] Before we wrap up, regarding the UAE, one name floated for the next UN Secretary-General is Lana Nusseibeh, an Emirati diplomat. After the UN accused the RSF of genocide, she dismissed the allegations. If she becomes Secretary-General, it could undermine confidence in international bodies. Any thoughts? [Speaker 3:] People see through it. Human rights organizations are making noise about this. Sudanese have a campaign against her appointment. If she’s allowed to become Secretary-General, it will erode trust in international bodies. The UN’s role in documenting atrocities is crucial, and her appointment would damage confidence in any Western body, even those with good intentions. [Speaker 2:] Thank you, Mossab, for your time and analysis. We look forward to speaking with you again soon. [Speaker 3:] Thank you, Ronnie and Zoe. Appreciate it.
